hypotheses.claim: Test synchronization race. When the first timestamped write is issued, the server's TLS 1.3 post-handshake NewSessionTicket records are still unread. The client is inside AsyncSocket::handleRead reading those tickets when the server's echo arrives carrying the TCP ACK. handleRead keeps looping and reads the echo without draining the socket error queue again, even though the ACK timestamp is already queued there. As a result, writeAndReflect returns before the ACK ByteEvent reaches the observer.
hypotheses.supporting: The FAIL has exactly 3 events (WRITE, SCHED, TX) and no ACK for offset 501. The second block passes, so the ACK was late, not lost. In the FAIL, the server handshake finishes before the client's first write; in the PASS it finishes after. The seed-11 syscall trace shows the server sending tickets (#90, #102) before the client's timestamped sendmsg (#3151). The client drains SCHED and TX; the error queue is empty when ioReady is entered (#3171). handleRead then reads ticket 1, ticket 2, and the echo (#3172-#3180) with no MSG_ERRQUEUE recvmsg in between. After write 2, the error queue yields 3 messages: the late ACK plus SCHED and TX. In the seed-1 PASS, the tickets carry the ACK and it is drained before any read. In AsyncSocket, ioReady calls handleErrMessages only on entry. The sibling test ObserverAttachedAfterConnect documents the same sequence and works around it the same way.
hypotheses.contradicting: No post-fix run exists, because the investigator cannot build. That the ACK timestamp is queued when the server echoes is inferred from how kernel TCP handles ACKs; the syscall trace does not observe it directly.
hypotheses.next_experiment: The controller builds the patched ELF, replays seeds 11 and 1 (both expected to PASS), and runs fresh seeds 12-15. In the post-fix trace, an error-queue read returning the ACK should come before the echo is read, and no ticket reads should follow the timestamped sendmsg.

hypotheses.claim: The kernel had not yet generated the ACK timestamp when the echo was read, for example because of delayed ACK on the server.
hypotheses.supporting: ACK is the only missing event type, and it depends on how the peer behaves.
hypotheses.contradicting: The server read the 'a' record before echoing it, so the echo segment must acknowledge offset 501, and the kernel processes the ACK before queueing the payload. The trace shows a late error-queue message drained after write 2, which fits a queued but unread ACK rather than a missing one.
hypotheses.next_experiment: In the FAIL schedule, add a recvmsg(MSG_ERRQUEUE) right after the echo is read. This hypothesis predicts EAGAIN; hypothesis 1 predicts the ACK for offset 501.

hypotheses.claim: Production defect: AsyncSocket should drain the error queue between reads inside handleRead.
hypotheses.supporting: It is the same mechanism: handleRead consumes data that arrived after the ACK timestamp was already queued.
hypotheses.contradicting: The event is delivered on the next ioReady (EPOLLERR is level-triggered), so it is not lost. The maintainers chose a test-side workaround for the identical sequence in the sibling test. The change would add a syscall to every read in the hot path.
hypotheses.next_experiment: Prototype handleErrMessages inside the handleRead loop, replay seed 11 without the test change, and measure the syscall overhead.

hypotheses.claim: Hermit artifact: chaos scheduling or epoll emulation hides EPOLLERR, or produces an interleaving that cannot happen natively.
hypotheses.supporting: The failure appears only under Hermit chaos scheduling with a particular seed.
hypotheses.contradicting: The interleaving is legal on native loopback. The sibling test's comment says the same sequence made that test flaky outside Hermit. The trace shows real error-queue reads returning the late ACK.
hypotheses.next_experiment: Run the unpatched test natively on a single contended core and look for the missing-ACK failure.

root_cause: Test synchronization race in ObserverAttachedBeforeConnect. TLS 1.3 NewSessionTickets are still unread when the first timestamped write is made; AsyncSocket handleRead consumes the tickets and then the echo in one loop without re-draining the error queue, where the ACK timestamp is already queued (ioReady drains it only on entry), so writeAndReflect returns before the ACK ByteEvent is delivered. Fix drains post-handshake data with an untimestamped writeAndReflect first.
